briefs.growing-pains:
Bilateral Leg Pain in a Child: Is the Examination Normal?

A normal exam is growing pains; tender calves after influenza are myositis

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Bilateral leg pain in a child: examine before you test.

  • Normal exam, episodic evening or night pain with pain-free days, age 3 to 12: growing pains. Reassure; no labs or films.
  • Tender calves days after an influenza-like illness: benign acute childhood myositis (influenza-induced myositis). CK (creatine kinase) is high and reflexes are preserved.
  • Ascending weakness with absent reflexes: Guillain-Barré syndrome.
  • Bone tenderness with pallor, bruising, fever or weight loss: CBC (complete blood count) with smear for leukemia.
  • One side, a focal tender spot or a mass: radiograph, even when night pain responds to NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs).

Night pain alone is not the flag; laterality, a limp, tenderness and systemic signs are.

Myositis can cause weakness (the NBME explanation: mild weakness to quadriparesis), so strength does not separate it from Guillain-Barré syndrome; preserved reflexes do, with calf tenderness and a high CK in support.

Diagnosis
Defining findings Growing pains – age 3 to 12; both legs (thighs, shins, calves), evenings or nights, worse after active days; pain-free days; pain in muscles, not joints; normal exam and gait; no systemic signs or activity limits · Myositis – influenza A or B, during or just after the illness; tender calves; tiptoe gait or refusal to walk; more often boys · Confirm – CK elevated; a positive influenza test names the cause
How NBME framed it: question 1

12-year-old boy with 2 days of severe pain in both calves a week ago: dry cough, sore throat, headache and fever all resolved on ibuprofen after 5 days; no medications now Marked tenderness of both calves T 37 °C

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Dermatomyositis: a myositis; but it brings proximal weakness with a heliotrope rash and Gottron papules; the stem describes no rash and no weakness.
  • Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease): the fever may have just reached its 5-day threshold; but it has resolved, with no conjunctivitis, rash, node, hand, foot or lip change. NBME used the formal name.
  • Parvovirus B19-induced arthritis: a post-viral ache; but it is symmetric arthritis of the small joints of the hands, wrists and feet; this tenderness is in muscle.
  • Rheumatic fever: a sore throat came first; but it follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis and is diagnosed by the Jones criteria (carditis, arthritis, nodules, erythema marginatum, chorea); calf tenderness is none of them.

Down to two: influenza-induced myositis or dermatomyositis. Influenza-induced myositis: tender calves a few days after a flu-like illness, with no rash or proximal weakness. The stem never names influenza, and the key names the cause rather than the syndrome.

Management and treatment
By situation Growing pains – explain the benign course; massage, heat, analgesics or stretching; no activity restriction or braces; recurrence is expected · Myositis – analgesia, fluids and rest; never aspirin with influenza (Reye syndrome) · Dark urine – heme on the dipstick, few red cells, high CK: rhabdomyolysis; admit for IV fluids; check creatinine and potassium
Practice
  1. 6-year-old boy, 3 months of pain in both thighs and shins only at night; worse after running days pain-free days; not worsening massage and ibuprofen help Walks, runs and plays normally Afebrile · no weight loss · hip and knee exam normal → Observation and reassurance → both legs, episodic night pain with pain-free days, a normal exam and no systemic signs: growing pains, a clinical diagnosis with no film or blood count
  2. 8-year-old boy with 2 months of right thigh pain at night wakes him; ibuprofen relieves it dramatically the left leg never hurts No mass or limp Afebrile · exam otherwise normal → Order plain radiographs → night pain on one side needs a film even when ibuprofen relieves it: osteoid osteoma also hurts at night and answers to NSAIDs
  3. 7-year-old girl with 3 weeks of leg pain that wakes her at night intermittent fevers pale, with scattered bruises Tender to palpation over both tibias T 38.1 °C · hip and knee motion full → Order a complete blood count with peripheral smear → bone tenderness with pallor, bruising and fever is not growing pains, which needs a normal exam: CBC with smear for leukemia
  4. 7-year-old boy was diagnosed with growing pains 2 weeks ago night leg pain after soccer days exam and gait normal Parents ask about stopping soccer or buying knee braces Afebrile · no weight loss → Continue normal activity without restriction → growing pains do not limit activity, and restriction and bracing are not recommended; reassure, and offer massage, heat, analgesics or stretching
  5. 9-year-old girl was diagnosed with growing pains 1 year ago still has night pain in both shins a few nights a month, with pain-free weeks Growing normally; plays sports Afebrile · joints and gait normal → Continued reassurance and supportive care → growing pains wax and wane for months to years and resolve by adolescence; recurrence with a normal exam is expected, not a reason to escalate
  6. 10-year-old boy with night leg pain his parents read that night pain means a tumor both shins hurt, worse after sports pain-free days; ibuprofen helps Exam and gait normal Afebrile · no weight loss → Osteoid osteoma is also nocturnal and also relieved by NSAIDs, so laterality is the discriminator → night pain and relief from NSAIDs are shared by growing pains and osteoid osteoma, so check the side, not the hour
  7. 7-year-old boy was diagnosed with influenza B 3 days ago now afebrile; woke refusing to walk walks on his toes both calves tender Strength normal when encouraged Knee and ankle reflexes normal · T 37.0 °C → Serum creatine kinase → tender calves with reflexes intact days into influenza: benign acute childhood myositis; an elevated CK places the problem in muscle
  8. 6-year-old boy on day 4 of influenza B, now afebrile pain in both calves; walks on tiptoe calves tender; strength and reflexes normal CK (creatine kinase) elevated T 37.2 °C · urinalysis normal → Analgesics, fluids and reassurance → myositis with a normal urinalysis: analgesia, fluids and rest at home; recovery within about a week
  9. 8-year-old girl with influenza A and 2 days of severe leg pain both calves tender tea-colored urine Urine dipstick strongly positive for blood T 37.4 °C · 0 to 2 red cells per high-power field · CK markedly elevated → Admission for intravenous fluids and renal monitoring → a heme-positive dipstick with almost no red cells and a markedly high CK is myoglobin: rhabdomyolysis; admit for intravenous fluids and follow creatinine and potassium
  10. 9-year-old boy with influenza, now afebrile pain in both calves for 2 days calves tender; strength and reflexes normal Parents ask what to give for the pain CK elevated · urinalysis normal → Aspirin → aspirin in a child with influenza risks Reye syndrome; give ibuprofen or acetaminophen
  11. 6-year-old boy with 2 days of leg pain upper respiratory infection 10 days ago trouble climbing stairs, now spreading upward symmetric leg weakness; no calf tenderness No sensory level; bladder normal Knee and ankle reflexes absent · T 37.0 °C → Guillain-Barré syndrome → ascending symmetric weakness with lost reflexes after an infection is Guillain-Barré syndrome: lumbar puncture and watch breathing; myositis keeps reflexes and hurts to touch
  12. 8-year-old girl with 2 months of trouble climbing stairs struggles to rise from the floor violaceous rash on both upper eyelids Scaly red papules over the knuckles CK elevated · T 37.0 °C → Juvenile dermatomyositis → weeks of proximal weakness with a heliotrope rash and Gottron papules is juvenile dermatomyositis: systemic glucocorticoids plus methotrexate
  13. 7-year-old girl with 4 months of aching in both calves evenings only, worse after active days pain-free days; no recent illness No calf tenderness; joints and gait normal Afebrile · no weight loss → Growing pains → episodic evening leg pain with pain-free days and a normal exam is growing pains; myositis follows influenza with tender calves, and arthritis swells joints
Pairs with The Limping Child: Sick or Well, Then Age and Time: the gait is abnormal. Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis: Keep Off It and Pin It: one-sided hip, thigh or knee pain in an adolescent. Pediatric Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia: the systemic picture. Hemoglobinuria: the Dipstick-Microscopy Mismatch: heme on the dipstick, no red cells.
Transferable rule

A frightening symptom shared by benign and serious causes is not the flag; find the feature that separates them. In leg pain, it is the exam and the side, not the hour.
